steps.name: Block in the cow

lines.text: Let the hills and the meadow, and the far mountains and the lake dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, measuring from the canvas edges with a ruler.
Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 2 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is about 1 1/4 in from the left edge; it's about 7 1/2 in wide and 9 in tall.
The outline also runs under where the meadow's tall grass and the horns' dark tips will go: paint straight through there.
The outline also reaches onto the green hills and meadow, and the dark bushes on the hills, painted already: there, only soften this paint into their edge and leave them showing.
Paint: Rust brown.
Mix enough Rust brown for this step and step 14; cover it between them.
Brush: 3/4 inch flat.
Start with the big oval of the body.
It should leave one solid Rust brown shape with a rough, hairy outline and no shading yet.

steps.meant: A flat rust-brown cow shape stands in the meadow, head to the right of its body. It has no shadows, no locks, no horns and no face.

steps.name: Shade the side away from the light

lines.text: Let the highland cow, and the hills and the meadow dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 3 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is about 1 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 7 in wide and 8 in tall.
The outline also runs under where the meadow's tall grass and the sunlit rim will go: paint straight through there.
The outline also reaches onto the green hills and meadow, and the highland cow, painted already: there, only soften this paint into their edge and leave them showing.
Paint: Dark umber.
Mix enough Dark umber for this step and steps 13 and 23; cover it between them.
Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
Bend every stroke with the hair: from the top of the back and the head, pull down along the curve of the body, putting the Dark umber only where the shadows fall on the Rust brown.
It should leave marks that bend with the shape, which is what makes it look round or sloped.

steps.meant: The rust cow has deep brown shadows down its left side, under its fringe and chin, and low on its body; the right side is still plain rust. It has no locks, horns or face.

steps.name: Block in the horns

lines.text: Let the cow's shadows and the highland cow dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, measuring from the canvas edges with a ruler.
Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 3 in from the top edge, and its right side is about 2 1/2 in from the right edge; it's about 6 1/2 in wide and 3 in tall.
Paint: Horn tan.
Brush: #6 round.
Paint each horn as one curved, tapering stroke: start wide where it meets the head and ease off the brush as you pull out to the tip.
It should leave two smooth pale horns, thick at the head and thin at the tips, with no shading yet.

steps.meant: Two flat pale tan horns curve up from the cow's head with no shading or dark tips. The coat is still rust and dark brown with no locks.

steps.name: Shade the horns and their tips

lines.text: Let the cow's horns and the cow's shadows dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 3 in from the top edge, and its right side is about 2 1/2 in from the right edge; it's about 6 in wide and 2 1/2 in tall.
Paint: Dark umber.
Brush: #4 round.
Bend every stroke with the horn: pull along its curve from the head out to the tip, adding more paint as you reach the tip.
It should leave marks that bend with the shape, which is what makes it look round or sloped.
Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

steps.meant: The horns have dark brown tips and undersides with the pale tan along their tops. The coat is still rust and dark brown with no locks.
